threads.thread_goal: Align on scope, success metrics, and initial call type mapping for the playbook.

messages.text: Kickoff for the Omnichannel Customer Service Playbook for Retail Contact Centre. Goal over the next 21 days is to get a usable v1 that works for phone, chat, and in-store, including bookshop. For this thread, can we align on: 1) top customer scenarios to prioritise (calls and in-store), 2) how we will measure success and where the data comes from. I will start mapping call types and escalation paths under T1 and capture them in A2 so we have a single view. Please share: - top 5 reasons customers contact us (phone/chat) - top 5 in-store scenarios you see most often - any existing reports you already use for satisfaction or first-contact resolution so we can feed into T12.

From the contact centre side, here are the most frequent ones I see on the floor: 1) Order status and delivery tracking 2) Returns and refunds 3) Product information before purchase (specs, compatibility, availability) 4) Account access issues (password reset, login problems) 5) Payment issues (failed payment, double charge) 6) Promo code or voucher issues 7) Complaints about damaged or wrong items 8) Loyalty points balance and redemption 9) Book availability and reservations 10) Store opening hours and stock in specific locations. For T1 and A2 I can help tag these with rough volumes and typical escalation paths based on recent weeks. For metrics, we already track average handling time, CSAT after calls, and a basic first-contact resolution flag in our current reports. Those should plug nicely into T12.

From the in-store side (non-bookshop), the main situations I see: 1) Customers asking which product fits their need (for example, which device or accessory) 2) Exchanges and returns for online orders brought into the store 3) Cross-store stock checks and reservations 4) Support with using products after purchase (set-up, basic troubleshooting) 5) Questions about warranties and extended service plans 6) Price match or promo clarification. I am not sure how we currently log these in a way that can feed into A2, since store systems are different. Maybe we can define a simple mapping so we can still include them in T1, even if volumes are more approximate.

For the bookshop specifically, the top scenarios I see in-store: 1) Recommendations based on reading preferences (genre, mood, age group) 2) Requests for a specific title or author, including out-of-stock checks 3) Special orders for publications we do not carry or that are out of print 4) Gift recommendations and bundles 5) Questions about events, signings, and pre-orders. Some of these overlap with what the contact centre gets via phone/chat, especially availability and special orders. It would be good if T1 and A2 reflect bookshop as a separate category so we can later link to the bookshop guidelines and examples in A4.

On success metrics for T12, I know we already have CSAT and call handling time, but I am not fully clear on how we measure first-contact resolution today. Is it based on a manual flag from agents or system logic? Also, for in-store, do we have any equivalent satisfaction measure, or will we need a simple paper or tablet survey during the pilot? I want to make sure whatever we define for T12 is realistic to track with current tools.

On first-contact resolution: today it is a manual flag in the call wrap-up screen. Not perfect, but it is what we can use immediately for T12. For in-store, we do not have a standard survey yet. For the pilot, we can use a short, two-question form and log results into a simple sheet that we later integrate into A2 or a separate tab. That keeps us within the constraint of using current tools. I will document this approach under T12 so we are explicit about data sources and limitations.

For the in-store scenarios you listed, we can probably mirror the contact centre categories so A2 stays consistent. For example: - Product fit questions map to product information before purchase - Exchanges and returns map to returns and refunds - Stock checks and reservations map to availability and reservations. For T1, I can draft a first pass of this mapping and share it so you can adjust wording to match how store teams talk about these situations.

That mapping sounds good. One nuance: in-store warranty questions often include upsell to extended plans, which is less common on the phone. Maybe we flag that as a sub-type so later, when we work on scripts, we remember to include the sales angle. I can review your T1 draft and add those sub-types before we finalise A2.

On the book-related call types you mentioned (availability, reservations, special orders), can we group them under a single bookshop category in A2 with sub-codes for: 1) title search, 2) recommendation, 3) special order? That will make it easier later to link to the dialogues we will add in A4. I can help define examples for each sub-code once T1 has the structure in place.

For the top 10 list, should we separate phone and chat, or treat them as one, since the reasons are similar? From what I see in reports, chat has more quick questions about store hours and promo codes, while phone has more complex issues like complaints and refunds. I am leaning to a single list with a channel column in A2, but open to other views.

I agree on a single list with a channel column in A2. That keeps T1 manageable and still lets us see differences by channel. For the top 10, based on what everyone shared and our existing reports, I propose this draft list: 1) Order status and delivery tracking 2) Returns and refunds (including exchanges) 3) Product information before purchase / product fit 4) Account access and login issues 5) Payment and billing issues 6) Promo code and voucher issues 7) Complaints about damaged or wrong items 8) Loyalty points and benefits 9) Bookshop: availability, recommendations, and special orders 10) In-store: stock checks, reservations, and store information. Please react or comment if anything critical is missing before we lock this as our focus for T1 and A2.

This list covers what I see most often. The only thing I would clarify is that complaints about damaged or wrong items often include a return or refund, but I think it is fine to keep them separate because the tone and handling are different. From my side, ok to use this as the top 10 for T1 and A2.

Happy with this list as well. The combined bookshop item gives us enough room to handle recommendations and special orders later in A4. No additional scenarios from my side that would push into the top 10.

From the store perspective, this list works. The in-store stock checks and reservations item will cover a lot of our daily interactions. I will just make sure we capture the warranty and extended plan questions as a sub-type when we refine A2. Ok to move forward with this top 10 for T1.

On success metrics for T12, summarising what we have so far: - Contact centre: CSAT after interaction, first-contact resolution flag, and average handling time - In-store: simple two-question pilot survey captured in a sheet, plus basic volume counts for the top 10 scenarios - Shared: we will also look at repeat contact rate for the same issue where we can identify it. All of this can be tracked with current reporting tools and simple sheets. Unless anyone sees a blocker, I suggest we confirm these as our initial success metrics and data sources for T12.

No blocker from me. Using existing CSAT, first-contact resolution, and handling time for the contact centre plus a simple in-store survey sounds practical. For the pilot, we can also add a quick question for agents and sellers about how easy the playbook is to use, and log that in the same sheet we will later use as input to A8.

Agree with this metric set. From an agent point of view, the first-contact resolution flag is already part of our routine, so no extra steps. For the in-store survey, we just need a very short format so it does not slow down queues. Ok to lock these as the initial success metrics for T12.

Closing this thread with two points: 1) We will use the proposed top 10 interaction types as the focus for T1 and A2, covering both contact centre and in-store, including bookshop. 2) We will track success using CSAT, first-contact resolution, handling time, repeat contact rate where available, and a simple in-store survey, all documented under T12. I will update A2 with the final list and channel mapping, and document the metric definitions and data sources in the T12 notes.

threads.thread_goal: Draft and iterate on standard call handling and quality monitoring approach.

messages.text: Sharing first drafts for our standard call handling and quality approach. Under T2, we now have version 0.8 of opening, verification, and closing scripts for phone and chat. Under T3, I added a draft quality monitoring scorecard and rubric, which will later live as A3. Both are linked in A1 as part of the playbook structure. Please use this thread to comment on: 1) wording and flow of the scripts, 2) whether the scorecard criteria and scoring rules are clear and practical, 3) anything missing for quick-reference checklists that we will build under T8 and A6. Aim is to converge on version 1.0 for both scripts and scorecard this week.

I went through the T2 scripts. Overall structure works well. A few detailed comments: - Opening: for phone, I suggest we add a short confirmation of the channel if the customer was transferred, for example, 'I see you were just chatting with us, thanks for continuing the conversation by phone.' That helps continuity. - Verification: we should be explicit about what to do if the customer refuses to share certain data, to stay aligned with privacy rules. Maybe a short alternative path in A1. - Closing: I would add a standard line to confirm if there is anything else we can help with before we mention the survey. I can propose exact wording and update T2 directly if that works.

On the T3 scorecard, I like that we separated soft skills, compliance, and resolution. I am a bit unsure about the weighting though. Right now, soft skills have more points than compliance. Given our constraints, should compliance have at least equal weight? Also, for the examples of good and bad behaviours in A3, could we add one example for handling an upset customer, since that is where tone and wording matter most?

Looking at the scripts in A1 from a store perspective, the chat opening feels a bit formal. In-store, we use more casual language, and I think some of that tone could help in chat as well. For example, instead of 'How may I assist you today', we could say 'How can I help you today'. Not a big change, but it sounds more natural. Also, for T8 and A6, I would like to see a short reminder about when it is appropriate to suggest a product or service, so agents do not feel they are pushing too hard.

From the bookshop angle, the general scripts in T2 work, but I would like to make sure we have a small variation for recommendation calls and chats. For example, after verification, a short question like 'What kind of books do you usually enjoy' would help us apply the later guidance in A4. Maybe we can add a bookshop-specific branch in A1 rather than changing the core script for everyone.

Good point on weighting. I agree compliance should not be lighter than soft skills. Proposal for T3 and A3: - Compliance: 40 percent - Resolution: 35 percent - Soft skills: 25 percent. That still values empathy and communication but makes it clear that following rules and actually solving the issue are non-negotiable. If no one objects, I will adjust the scorecard and rubric accordingly.

I support that weighting. From coaching sessions, most serious issues come from compliance or incomplete resolution, not from slightly imperfect phrasing. The proposed split for T3 and A3 reflects that. I will also add one or two examples of how to keep empathy while still following verification rules, so agents see how to balance both.

The new weighting works for me. For the upset customer example in A3, I can draft a short scenario where the customer received the wrong item twice, and show what a good apology and resolution look like versus a poor one. I will add that under T3 and flag it for your review.

I have now updated T2 with: - a transfer continuity line in the opening for phone - a short alternative path when the customer does not want to share certain data, pointing to what we can and cannot do in that case - a standard 'anything else' check before we mention the survey in the closing. Please have a quick look and confirm if we can treat this as version 1.0 of the opening, verification, and closing scripts, so we can reference them in A1 and start building A6 and T8 on top.

I reviewed your updates in T2. The flow reads well, and the alternative path for limited verification is clear and aligned with our constraints. I also added a small note in A1 to highlight the bookshop-specific branch we will plug in later, as suggested earlier. From my side, we can treat the current T2 scripts as version 1.0 for opening, verification, and closing.

I also checked the updated T2 scripts. The tone feels natural for both phone and chat, and the closing now clearly invites any last questions before we mention the survey. I am comfortable using this as our standard going forward.

Thanks for adding the note in A1. Once we move to the bookshop guidelines in A4, I will propose a short set of questions that can plug into the verification and discovery part of T2 for book-related calls and chats. That way, we keep the structure consistent but still make space for tailored recommendations.

I have incorporated the new weighting and examples into T3 and updated A3 accordingly. The scorecard now clearly shows: - Compliance: 40 percent - Resolution: 35 percent - Soft skills: 25 percent. Unless there are strong objections, I suggest we confirm this as our final quality monitoring scorecard criteria and scoring rules so we can start using it in coaching and in the quick-reference materials under A6 and T8.
Confirmed from my side. The criteria and scoring rules in T3 and A3 are clear, and the examples make it easier to calibrate between supervisors. Ready to use this version in our monitoring sessions.
Agree as well. The updated A3 is straightforward to explain to the team, and the weighting reflects what we want to reinforce. I will start using this scorecard in my next round of call reviews.

To wrap up this thread: - We have agreed on version 1.0 of the standard opening, verification, and closing scripts under T2, now referenced in A1 and ready to feed into A6 and T8. - We have agreed on the final quality monitoring scorecard criteria and scoring rules under T3, captured in A3 with updated weighting and examples. Next step is to translate these into concise checklists under T8 so agents and sellers have one-page references during live interactions.

threads.thread_goal: Define in-store specialised seller and bookshop-specific guidelines.

messages.text: Kicking off the in-store and bookshop guidelines thread. I have drafted initial sales and cross-sell scripts for specialised sellers under T4, which will later become part of A5. They cover five common scenarios: 1) Customer looking for a specific product 2) Customer unsure which product fits their need 3) Customer coming in with an online order issue 4) Customer asking about warranties or service plans 5) Customer browsing and open to suggestions. For each, I added a simple structure: understand need, propose main solution, suggest one relevant cross-sell, and confirm satisfaction. Please review and comment, especially on tone and how this should align with the general principles in A1 and the quick-reference format in A6.

Thanks for sharing the T4 drafts. For the bookshop side, I see a lot of overlap in structure, but the content is obviously different. Under T5, I started a checklist for understanding reading preferences and a process for special orders, which will feed into A4. I suggest we keep the same high-level flow you used: understand need, propose main title, suggest one or two alternatives or related items, and confirm if the customer is satisfied or needs something else. That way, A4 and A5 feel consistent even though the examples differ.

I went through the T4 scripts. The structure is solid, but I want to make sure we stay aligned with the overall service principles in A1. Two points: 1) In the online order issue scenario, the script should first focus on resolving the problem before any cross-sell suggestion. Right now, the cross-sell comes a bit early. 2) For warranties and service plans, we should include a short reminder to check eligibility and not oversell something that does not fit the customer profile. I can help adjust the wording so it matches the tone we use in the contact centre.

From the contact centre side, I like that your T4 scripts mirror the call flow we defined earlier. One suggestion: in the scenario where the customer is just browsing, maybe we can add a short discovery question similar to what we use on calls, like 'What are you mainly using this for'. That helps avoid generic suggestions. Also, for A6, it would be useful if the in-store checklist highlights one or two phrases that clearly signal we are not pushing, for example, 'If it makes sense for you, we also have...'.

Good catch on the online order issue scenario. I will rework that script in T4 so the cross-sell only appears after the issue is fully resolved and the customer confirms they are satisfied. For warranties, I will add a short step to check eligibility and a reminder not to offer plans that do not match the product or usage. Once I update T4, I will ping you for a quick review before we call A5 stable.

On T5, I have now added: - a checklist for reading preferences (genre, pace, tone, previous favourites, format) - a step-by-step for special orders, including how to handle out-of-print titles and how to set expectations on delivery times - ten example dialogues for different customer types, which will form the core of A4. Please review and let me know if there are any gaps from the store perspective, especially where bookshop and general store flows intersect.

I reviewed the T5 content. The preference checklist and special order process are clear and practical. The dialogues in A4 also show a good balance between guidance and not overwhelming the customer. From a contact centre view, the only addition I would suggest is a short note on how to handle data privacy when taking contact details for special orders, so we stay aligned with our constraints. Once that is in, I think we can treat the T5 guidelines as ready for approval.

I have added a short section in T5 on how to explain why we need contact details for special orders, what we will use them for, and how long we keep them, in line with our current policies. The dialogues in A4 now include one example where the customer asks about data use, so sellers can see how to respond clearly. With that, I am comfortable with the guidelines as they stand.

I updated the browsing scenario in T4 to include a discovery question similar to what you suggested. I also added a phrase like 'If it is helpful, we also have...' to make the cross-sell feel optional. For A5, I will highlight these phrases so they are easy to spot. Could you and 291562 confirm if the updated T4 scripts are good enough to be our core set for specialised sellers, so we can move them into A5 as version 1.0

I checked the latest T4 version. The discovery questions and softer cross-sell phrasing work well and are consistent with what we use on calls. From my side, these scripts are ready to be treated as the core set for specialised sellers and moved into A5 as version 1.0.

I also reviewed the updated T4 scripts. The order of steps now clearly prioritises solving the customer issue before any suggestion, and the eligibility reminder for warranties is clear. I am comfortable approving these as our core sales and cross-sell scripts for specialised sellers and capturing them in A5.

With the privacy note and example now added to T5 and A4, I think the bookshop recommendation and special order guidelines are complete for this phase. They cover preference discovery, special order handling, and clear examples of dialogues. Unless anyone sees a major gap, I suggest we approve these guidelines so they can be integrated into the main playbook.

Agreed. The current T5 and A4 content reflect how we already work in the bookshop, with clearer structure and examples. I do not see any major gaps for the pilot. Happy to move forward with these as our approved guidelines.

From the contact centre side, the T5 guidelines and A4 dialogues are also usable for phone and chat when we get book-related contacts. They align with the verification and discovery flow we already defined. I support approving them as part of the playbook.

To summarise this thread: - We have approved the core sales and cross-sell scripts for specialised sellers under T4, now captured in A5 as version 1.0. - We have approved the bookshop recommendation and special order guidelines under T5, documented in A4 with checklists and example dialogues. Next step is to ensure both A4 and A5 are reflected in the quick-reference checklists in A6 and in the consolidated playbook structure in A1.

threads.thread_goal: Consolidate the omnichannel playbook and align on shared principles.

messages.text: I have put together a draft table of contents for the Omnichannel Customer Service Playbook in A1, pulling in the work from A2, A3, A4, and A5, and linking to tasks T6, T7, and T11. The structure includes: 1) Omnichannel service principles 2) Standard call and chat flows 3) In-store and specialised seller flows 4) Bookshop-specific guidance 5) Quality monitoring and coaching 6) Quick-reference checklists. In this thread, I would like us to: - agree on the final set of shared service principles across channels for T6 - check for gaps or overlaps in the table of contents before we move to T7 and legal review under T11.

Looking at the draft in A1, the structure feels logical from an agent perspective. For the shared service principles under T6, I suggest we include at least: - Resolve the main issue before suggesting anything additional - Use clear, simple language and avoid jargon - Confirm understanding and next steps before closing - Protect customer data and explain why we ask for information - Keep tone consistent across channels, even if wording changes slightly. These should apply to phone, chat, and in-store, including bookshop.

From the store side, I would add two more principles to T6: - Make relevant suggestions, not generic ones, and only when they add value - Adapt to the customer pace, especially in-store where some people want to browse quietly. Also, in the table of contents in A1, maybe we should call out a short section on how to move a customer between channels smoothly, for example, from chat to store or from store to contact centre.

For bookshop, the principles you listed already fit well. I would just emphasise one more for T6: - Start from the customer interests, not from the product we want to promote. That is already reflected in A4, but it would be good to see it in the shared principles section too. On the table of contents, I do not see any major gaps for bookshop content; A4 is well placed under the bookshop-specific chapter.

I like the idea of a section on moving between channels. In A1, maybe under omnichannel principles, we can add a short subsection on handovers, with examples like: - how to summarise the situation when sending a customer from chat to phone - what information to give a customer who is going from contact centre to store. For T6, I would also include something about setting realistic expectations on timing, especially for deliveries and special orders.

Combining all suggestions, here is a proposed list of shared service principles for T6: 1) Resolve the main issue before suggesting anything additional 2) Use clear, simple language and avoid jargon 3) Confirm understanding and next steps before closing 4) Protect customer data and explain why we ask for information 5) Make relevant suggestions that add value, not generic ones 6) Adapt to the customer pace and channel 7) Start from the customer interests, not from what we want to promote 8) Set realistic expectations on timing and follow-up 9) Ensure smooth handovers between channels with clear summaries. Please react or comment; if we agree, I will document these in T6 and integrate them into A1.

This list captures what we need. It is short enough to remember and broad enough to cover both contact centre and in-store. From my side, ok to treat these as the final shared principles for T6 and A1.
Agreed as well. The focus on customer interests and realistic expectations is especially important for bookshop, and it is good to see it explicitly listed. Happy to move forward with this set.
No objections from me. These principles will be easy to explain to store teams and match the scripts we have in A5. I will make sure we reference them at the top of the in-store section in A1.

I have now updated T6 with the agreed principles and integrated them into the opening chapter of A1. Next, I walked through the table of contents against A2, A3, A4, and A5 to check for gaps. Everything we defined so far is represented. The only small addition I made is a short subsection under quality monitoring to explain how the scorecard in A3 applies to both calls and in-store interactions, with examples from each.

I reviewed the updated A1 table of contents and the new subsection on applying A3 to in-store. It reads clearly. I do not see any missing pieces from the contact centre or store perspective. For T7, I think we are ready to say that all approved scripts, workflows, and guidelines are consolidated in A1 for v1.0, pending the legal and data privacy review under T11.

From an agent view, the consolidated A1 is easy to navigate. The quick-reference section points clearly to A6, and the links to A2, A3, A4, and A5 are intuitive. I agree with 504375 that we can treat this as playbook v1.0 content, as long as we still run the full legal and privacy check under T11 before the pilot.

I will now run through T11 with our compliance contact to check all scripts and workflows in A1 against the existing checklist. I will not change any system behaviour, only wording where needed. Once we have sign-off, we can formally mark A1 as playbook v1.0 for the pilot.

Compliance review under T11 is now complete. A few minor phrasing changes were made in A1, A4, and A5 to clarify data use and avoid any misleading wording around warranties. No structural changes. With that, I propose we sign off on A1 as playbook v1.0 content for the pilot rollout.
Confirmed from my side. The updated A1 still reads clearly, and the compliance tweaks do not change the intent. Ready to use this as v1.0 in the pilot.
I checked the changes in A4 and A5 related to bookshop and in-store. The clarifications are sensible and do not add complexity for sellers. I am comfortable signing off on A1 as v1.0 for the pilot.
All good from my side as well. The consolidated A1 reflects what we have been working on, and the legal review under T11 gives me confidence for the pilot. Happy to sign off on v1.0.

Closing this thread: - We agreed on the final set of omnichannel service principles under T6 and integrated them into A1. - We consolidated all approved scripts, workflows, and guidelines into A1 as playbook v1.0, with compliance review completed under T11. This gives us a solid base to move into pilot training and feedback in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot training, collect feedback, and define next iteration.

messages.text: With A1 signed off as playbook v1.0, we can move to the pilot. Under T9, I have drafted a pilot training plan and added it to A7, including proposed dates and target teams in the contact centre and stores. Under T10, we will use A8 to capture feedback and decide what goes into playbook v1.1. In this thread, we need to: 1) confirm pilot scope, participating teams, and training dates 2) agree on how we will collect and prioritise feedback for the next iteration, aligned with T12 metrics.

Looking at A7, the proposed pilot scope is: - Contact centre: one weekday team and one weekend team - Stores: two high-traffic stores and one smaller store, plus the main bookshop. This seems balanced. On dates, the plan shows training sessions next week, with follow-up coaching the week after. From my side, that timing works, but we need to make sure we have enough supervisors available for live support during the first days.

For the contact centre teams listed in A7, I can help run short refreshers at the start of each shift during the first pilot week, focusing on the new scripts and the quick-reference checklists in A6. That should reduce confusion. On dates, the proposed schedule works for my team, as long as we get the final training materials at least one day in advance.

For the stores in A7, I suggest we double-check that the high-traffic locations have enough coverage during training. Maybe we can schedule sessions just before opening or right after closing to avoid long queues. I can coordinate with store managers to confirm the dates in T9. Also, for feedback, I would like a simple way for sellers to log quick comments right after interactions, not only at the end of the week.

For the bookshop, the proposed dates in A7 are fine. We usually have quieter periods mid-morning, so we can schedule training then. For feedback into A8, I can collect both structured feedback using the form in T10 and a few short examples of customer reactions to the new recommendation flow, so we see how it lands in practice.

Based on your comments, I propose we confirm the pilot scope as: - Contact centre: one weekday and one weekend team - Stores: two high-traffic stores, one smaller store, and the main bookshop. Training dates as per A7 next week, with short shift refreshers and follow-up coaching the week after. I will update T9 accordingly and send calendar invites. Please confirm if you are ok with this scope and timing so we can lock it in.
Ok for me. The mix of teams and stores will give us a good view of different patterns. I will make sure supervisors are available for live support during the first two pilot days.
Confirmed from the contact centre side. The dates and scope in A7 work, and I will prepare short shift huddles to reinforce the key points from A6 and A1.
Scope and dates look good for the selected stores. I will coordinate with store managers to confirm exact training slots and update T9 once we have them.
All good for the bookshop as well. I will block time for the team and make sure they have printed copies of the key pages from A4 and A6 during the first pilot days.

On feedback collection under T10 and A8, here is a proposal: - Structured feedback form with a few questions on clarity, usefulness, and ease of use of A1 and A6, plus space for suggestions - Quick free-text log where agents and sellers can note specific interactions where the playbook helped or got in the way - Weekly summary of key themes, linked to T12 metrics where possible (for example, if a change seems to reduce handling time or improve first-contact resolution). We would then review all feedback after the pilot and decide which changes go into playbook v1.1.

That approach works for agents. If the feedback form is short, we can fill it at the end of the shift. For the free-text log in A8, I can add a few examples from calls where the new scripts made a clear difference, positive or negative, so we have concrete cases to discuss when deciding on v1.1 changes.

For stores, I will encourage sellers to log at least one example per day in A8, even if it is just a short note. That should give us enough variety. When we review for v1.1, I suggest we prioritise changes that: - remove confusion or repeated questions from staff - clearly support the T12 metrics, like improving first-contact resolution or satisfaction.

For bookshop, I will focus feedback in A8 on: - how easy it is to use the recommendation checklist from A4 during real conversations - whether customers react positively to the new questions and suggestions. When we decide what goes into v1.1, I would like to keep any changes that clearly help us find better matches faster, even if they are small wording tweaks.

On prioritising improvements for v1.1, I suggest we use three simple categories in A8: 1) Must-change before wider rollout (for example, anything that creates confusion or risk) 2) Should-change soon (clear benefits, low effort) 3) Nice-to-have (good ideas but not critical for now). That will help us decide what we include in the next version without overloading the team.

Agreed on the three categories. For deciding what goes into playbook v1.1, I propose we include: - all must-change items - should-change items that either support T12 targets or are quick wins - defer nice-to-have items unless they are very low effort. We will document the final list of changes in A8 and then update A1 accordingly after the pilot.
That selection rule makes sense. It keeps us focused on safety, clarity, and measurable impact. I am ok using this approach to decide which improvements go into v1.1.
I agree as well. For bookshop, most changes will probably be in the should-change category, and we can pick the ones that clearly help with T12 satisfaction and resolution goals.

To close this thread: - We confirmed the pilot scope, participating teams, and training dates as documented in A7 and T9, covering contact centre, stores, and bookshop. - We agreed on how to collect and categorise feedback in A8 under T10, and on the criteria for selecting which improvements go into playbook v1.1, aligned with T12 metrics. Next steps are to run the training sessions, start logging feedback, and then plan the v1.1 update after the pilot period.
